v.why: A 3x3 conv on 1->3 gains little when node 1 receives no input because edge 0 is severed.
A conv on 2->3 is worth less when its upstream edge 1 is none, since node 2 then carries only weak or no signal.
Stacked 3x3 convs on route 0->1->3 compound receptive field and capacity.
Adding a residual shortcut where no direct path existed gives a larger gain than replacing an existing parameter-free op.
Replacing none with a conv adds new capacity and a direct path, a bigger gain than swapping skip_connect for conv.
Adding a conv where the edge was absent brings new capacity and connectivity, more than replacing skip_connect.
Severing edge 0 is catastrophic when edge 1 is also none, since the input is then disconnected from most routes.
Removing edge 5 costs less when a strong conv on edge 4 already supplies node 3 with features.
The bridge 1->2 is more dispensable when edge 1 already feeds node 2 with a conv path.
A shortcut on 0->3 is redundant and adds less when a competing conv route into node 3 is present.

raw:
The literature search returned nothing relevant (power electronics, ecology, networking), so these hypotheses rest on prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 rather than on citations.

Reasoning behind the choices:
- Edge 3 is the direct 0->3 route. When the other routes into node 3 are weak, a conv on edge 3 matters more, so edge 3 conv edits should gain more when the competing routes are poor.
- Upgrading edge 4 or 5 to conv should gain more when its upstream edge is also a conv. A 3x3 conv on 1->3 does little if edge 0 is none, and more if edge 0 is a conv. The saturation counter-hypothesis is less likely, so I lean toward complementarity.
- Replacing 'none' with a conv gives a larger gain than replacing skip_connect, because skip already provides a trainable path.
- Setting an edge to none is costlier when no sibling conv edge can compensate.
